claim: The study measured mRNA and protein levels in genetically diverse mice at ages 6, 12, and 18 months.
source: In order to better understand these changes, we measured mRNA and protein levels in genetically diverse mice at different ages.
evidence: The abstract and methods sections describe the experimental design measuring both mRNA and protein at three age time points.

claim: Changes in both mRNA and protein are associated with increased immune infiltration.
source: Changes in both mRNA and protein are associated with increased immune infiltration and decreases in mitochondrial function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: Changes in both mRNA and protein are associated with decreases in mitochondrial function.
source: Changes in both mRNA and protein are associated with increased immune infiltration and decreases in mitochondrial function.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: Proteins show a greater extent of change compared to mRNA with age.
source: Proteins show a greater extent of change and reveal changes in a wide array of biological processes including unique, organ-specific features of aging in kidney.
evidence: The abstract makes this claim, supported by comparative analysis of mRNA and protein changes in the results section.

claim: Functionally important age-related changes in protein occur in the absence of corresponding changes in mRNA.
source: Most importantly, we observed functionally important age-related changes in protein that occur in the absence of corresponding changes in mRNA.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by mediation analysis and comparison of mRNA-protein concordance in the results.

claim: mRNA profiling alone provides an incomplete picture of molecular aging in the kidney.
source: Our findings suggest that mRNA profiling alone provides an incomplete picture of molecular aging in the kidney and that examination of changes in proteins is essential to understand aging processes that are not transcriptionally regulated.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing discordance between mRNA and protein changes.

claim: Kidney function declines progressively with age.
source: Kidney function is affected early in the aging process and declines progressively with age.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Glomerular filtration rate declines by 5-10% per decade after age 35 in humans.
source: Decreased renal volume and the loss of functioning filtration units lead to a decline in glomerular filtration rate of 5–10% per decade after the age of 35 in humans (Glassock and Rule, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Glassock and Rule, 2012.

claim: Kidney function significantly impacts age-related diseases in other organs including cognitive impairment.
source: Moreover, kidney function significantly impacts age-related diseases in other organs including cognitive impairment (Elias et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elias et al., 2009.

claim: Previous molecular profiling studies of the aging kidney have been limited to microarray based gene expression assays in young versus old kidneys of mice and rats.
source: Previous molecular profiling studies of the aging kidney have been limited to microarray based gene expression assays in young versus old kidneys of mice and rats (Jonker et al., 2013; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jonker et al., 2013 and Park et al., 2016.

claim: Single cell transcriptional profiling of aging C57BL/6NJ mice has been reported for multiple tissues, including kidney.
source: More recently, single cell transcriptional profiling of aging C57BL/6NJ mice has been reported for multiple tissues, including kidney (Almanzar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Almanzar et al., 2020.

claim: Studies carried out in single inbred strains may display specific and idiosyncratic patterns of aging and lack generalizability.
source: When aging studies are carried out in single inbred strains, they may display specific and idiosyncratic patterns of aging and thus lack generalizability beyond the particular strain studied (Voelkl et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Voelkl et al., 2020.

claim: The study examined approximately 600 DO mice including equal numbers of male and female mice.
source: We carried out a cross-sectional aging study of ~600 DO mice including equal numbers of male and female mice that were aged to 6, 12, and 18 months.
evidence: The experimental design section describes the cohort size and composition.

claim: Spot urine was successfully collected from 490 mice.
source: To evaluate kidney function, we successfully collected spot urine from 490 mice (141 at 6 months, 199 at 12 months, and 150 at 18 months) and measured albumin, creatinine, and phosphate levels.
evidence: The experimental design section reports the number of urine samples collected.

claim: The study quantified mRNA by RNA-Seq and detected expression of 22,259 genes.
source: We quantified mRNA by RNA-Seq and detected expression of 22,259 genes.
evidence: The experimental design section reports the number of genes detected by RNA-Seq.

claim: The study obtained untargeted proteomics data and quantified 6580 proteins representing 6515 unique genes.
source: We obtained untargeted proteomics data on the same set of 188 kidney samples and quantified 6580 proteins representing 6515 unique genes.
evidence: The experimental design section reports the number of proteins quantified.

claim: Both mRNA and protein data were available for 6449 genes.
source: Both mRNA and protein data were available for 6449 genes.
evidence: The experimental design section reports the overlap between mRNA and protein data.

claim: The top four PCs for RNA explain 46.5% of variance.
source: The top four PCs for RNA explain 46.5% of variance (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The first PC for RNA explains 22.1% of variance and is strongly correlated with sex (p-value <2.2 × 10−16).
source: The first PC explains 22.1% of variance and is strongly correlated with sex (p-value <2.2 × 10−16) and only weakly correlated with age (p-value = 0.050).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of RNA data.

claim: The first PC for RNA is only weakly correlated with age (p-value = 0.050).
source: The first PC explains 22.1% of variance and is strongly correlated with sex (p-value <2.2 × 10−16) and only weakly correlated with age (p-value = 0.050).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of RNA data.

claim: The second PC for RNA explains 15.3% of total variance and is not associated with sex (p-value = 0.30) or with age (p-value = 0.87).
source: The second PC (PC2) explains 15.3% of total variance and is not associated with sex (p-value = 0.30) or with age (p-value = 0.87).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of RNA data.

claim: PC2 for RNA is explained by a batch effect in the RNA sequencing.
source: PC2 is explained by a batch effect in the RNA sequencing that we account for in subsequent analyses (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of RNA data.

claim: Sex is a dominant factor in determining mRNA variation with minor contribution attributable to age.
source: Overall sex is a dominant factor in determining mRNA variation with minor contribution attributable to age.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the principal component analysis of RNA data.

claim: The top four PCs for protein explain 39.1% of total variation.
source: The top four PCs for protein explain 39.1% of total variation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The first PC for protein explains 16.6% and is strongly associated with age (p-value = 5.3 × 10−14) but not with sex (p-value = 0.24).
source: The first PC explains 16.6% and is strongly associated with age (p-value = 5.3 × 10−14) but not with sex (p-value = 0.24).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of protein data.

claim: The second PC for protein explains 12.0% of variation and is associated with sex (p-value < 2.2 × 10−16) and only marginally so with age (p-value = 0.014).
source: The second PC explains 12.0% of variation. It is associated with sex (p-value < 2.2 × 10−16) and only marginally so with age (p-value = 0.014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing principal component analysis of protein data.

claim: Age is a dominant factor in determining protein variation with lesser but still substantial influence due to sex.
source: In contrast to mRNA, age is a dominant factor in determining protein variation with lesser but still substantial influence due to sex.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the principal component analysis of protein data.

claim: The age-specific variability of the protein PCs is greater in the 18-month animals indicating greater between-animal variation in protein at later ages.
source: We also observed that the age-specific variability of the protein PCs (especially PC1 and PC4) is greater in the 18-month animals indicating that there is greater between-animal variation in protein at later ages.
evidence: This observation is made from the principal component analysis of protein data.

claim: Variation of mRNA is constant across age groups.
source: In contrast, variation of mRNA is constant across age groups.
evidence: This observation is made from the principal component analysis of mRNA data.

claim: 449 transcripts showed a trend with age (adjusted p-value < 0.05).
source: We identified 449 transcripts that showed a trend with age (adjusted p-value < 0.05) of which 426 show increasing expression with age and only 23 are decreasing.
evidence: This is reported from differential expression testing with DESeq2.

claim: 426 transcripts show increasing expression with age and only 23 are decreasing (adjusted p-value < 0.05).
source: We identified 449 transcripts that showed a trend with age (adjusted p-value < 0.05) of which 426 show increasing expression with age and only 23 are decreasing.
evidence: This is reported from differential expression testing with DESeq2.

claim: 95% of the age-related transcript changes are increasing at stringent family-wise criterion.
source: It is striking that 95% of the changes are increasing, but this is a stringent family-wise criterion that selects only transcripts with the biggest age-related changes.
evidence: This is calculated from the differential expression results.

claim: At FDR < 0.1, 4039 transcripts change with age and 2649 (65%) are increasing.
source: At a relaxed stringency using a false discovery rate criterion (FDR < 0.1), we identified 4039 transcripts that change with age and 2649 (65%) are increasing.
evidence: This is reported from differential expression testing with a relaxed threshold.

claim: Among the 426 mRNA species with the largest increase with age, 83 are immunoglobulin genes (Igh and Igk classes).
source: The 426 mRNA species with the largest increase with age, we find 83 immunoglobulin genes (Igh and Igk classes).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of the genes with significant age-related increases.

claim: The 23 decreasing mRNA species include several that encode heat shock proteins (Hsp90aa1, Hsp90ab1, Hsph1, and Hspa4l).
source: The 23 decreasing mRNA species include several that encode heat shock proteins (Hsp90aa1, Hsp90ab1, Hsph1, and Hspa4l).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of the genes with significant age-related decreases.

claim: Genes associated with adaptive immune response are significantly overrepresented (adjusted p-value = 1.3 × 10−23).
source: We observed significant overrepresentation of genes associated with adaptive immune response (adjusted p-value = 1.3 × 10−23), leukocyte activation (adjusted p-value = 4.9 × 10−25), and leukocyte cell–cell adhesion (adjusted p-value = 1.4 × 10−16).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis using ClusterProfiler.

claim: Genes associated with leukocyte activation are significantly overrepresented (adjusted p-value = 4.9 × 10−25).
source: We observed significant overrepresentation of genes associated with adaptive immune response (adjusted p-value = 1.3 × 10−23), leukocyte activation (adjusted p-value = 4.9 × 10−25), and leukocyte cell–cell adhesion (adjusted p-value = 1.4 × 10−16).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis using ClusterProfiler.

claim: Genes associated with leukocyte cell-cell adhesion are significantly overrepresented (adjusted p-value = 1.4 × 10−16).
source: We observed significant overrepresentation of genes associated with adaptive immune response (adjusted p-value = 1.3 × 10−23), leukocyte activation (adjusted p-value = 4.9 × 10−25), and leukocyte cell–cell adhesion (adjusted p-value = 1.4 × 10−16).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis using ClusterProfiler.

claim: All of the top 100 enrichment categories were related to immune cell functions.
source: All of the top 100 enrichment categories were related to immune cell functions.
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Increased expression of immune and inflammatory response genes in the aging kidney is likely the result of immune cell infiltration into the kidney.
source: Increased expression of immune and inflammatory response genes in the aging kidney has been shown in previous mRNA expression studies and is likely the result of immune cell infiltration into the kidney (Rodwell et al., 2004; Melk et al., 2005a; Park et al., 2016).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous studies and by the current data.

claim: There is a significant increase in B cell proportion with age (adjusted p = 6.75 × 10−6).
source: We found a significant increase in B cell proportion (adjusted p = 6.75 × 10−6) as well as macrophage proportion (adjusted p-value = 0.0155) with age in both sexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is reported from in silico cell type deconvolution analysis.

claim: There is a significant increase in macrophage proportion with age (adjusted p-value = 0.0155).
source: We found a significant increase in B cell proportion (adjusted p = 6.75 × 10−6) as well as macrophage proportion (adjusted p-value = 0.0155) with age in both sexes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is reported from in silico cell type deconvolution analysis.

claim: Cdkn2a shows increasing expression with age (adjusted p-value = 6.1 × 10−9).
source: Among the mRNA with most significant age-related changes, we noted increasing expression of Cdkn2a (adjusted p-value = 6.1 × 10−9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is reported from differential expression analysis.

claim: p16 (or p16INK4a) encoded by Cdkn2a is a hallmark for senescence.
source: One of the two proteins encoded by Cdkn2a, p16 (or p16INK4a) is a hallmark for senescence (Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018.

claim: Cdkn2a is highly expressed in the renal cortex and associated with severity of age-associated glomerulosclerosis, tubular damage, and interstitial fibrosis.
source: In an in vivo study, Cdkn2a was found to be highly expressed in the renal cortex and associated with severity of age-associated glomerulosclerosis, tubular damage, and interstitial fibrosis (Melk et al., 2005b; Bolignano et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Melk et al., 2005b and Bolignano et al., 2014.

claim: 876 proteins change with age (adjusted p-value < 0.05).
source: We identified 876 proteins that change with age (adjusted p-value < 0.05) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is reported from linear mixed model ANOVA analysis of protein data.

claim: Of the 876 proteins that change with age, 352 increased and 524 decreased.
source: Of these, 352 increased with age and 524 decreased.
evidence: This is reported from linear mixed model ANOVA analysis of protein data.

claim: HIST1H1B and other histones are decreasing with age.
source: Proteins with the most significant age trends include HIST1H1B and other histones that are decreasing with age; increasing ACTA2 a marker gene for myofibroblasts and indicator of renal fibrosis (Duffield, 2014); decreasing NCLN, which is part of a complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (Haffner et al., 2007); and decreasing CISD2, which is involved in mitochondrial autophagy (Chen et al., 2009; Figure 3).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of proteins with significant age trends.

claim: ACTA2, a marker gene for myofibroblasts and indicator of renal fibrosis, is increasing with age.
source: Proteins with the most significant age trends include HIST1H1B and other histones that are decreasing with age; increasing ACTA2 a marker gene for myofibroblasts and indicator of renal fibrosis (Duffield, 2014); decreasing NCLN, which is part of a complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (Haffner et al., 2007); and decreasing CISD2, which is involved in mitochondrial autophagy (Chen et al., 2009; Figure 3).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of proteins with significant age trends, with citation to Duffield, 2014.

claim: NCLN, which is part of a complex in the endoplasmic reticulum, is decreasing with age.
source: Proteins with the most significant age trends include HIST1H1B and other histones that are decreasing with age; increasing ACTA2 a marker gene for myofibroblasts and indicator of renal fibrosis (Duffield, 2014); decreasing NCLN, which is part of a complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (Haffner et al., 2007); and decreasing CISD2, which is involved in mitochondrial autophagy (Chen et al., 2009; Figure 3).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of proteins with significant age trends, with citation to Haffner et al., 2007.

claim: CISD2, which is involved in mitochondrial autophagy, is decreasing with age.
source: Proteins with the most significant age trends include HIST1H1B and other histones that are decreasing with age; increasing ACTA2 a marker gene for myofibroblasts and indicator of renal fibrosis (Duffield, 2014); decreasing NCLN, which is part of a complex in the endoplasmic reticulum (Haffner et al., 2007); and decreasing CISD2, which is involved in mitochondrial autophagy (Chen et al., 2009; Figure 3).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of proteins with significant age trends, with citation to Chen et al., 2009.

claim: 186 GO terms are overrepresented among age-changing proteins (adjusted p-value < 0.01).
source: We evaluated the proteins for functional enrichment of GO categories using ClusterProfiler and observed overrepresentation of genes associated with 186 terms (adjusted p-value < 0.01) representing a wide array of biological processes, cellular compartments, and molecular functions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis using ClusterProfiler.

claim: Proteins associated with oxidative phosphorylation show a general pattern of decrease with age (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8).
source: We observed a general pattern of decrease with age for protein associated with oxidative phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8) and the mitochondrial membrane (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12), as well as protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5), glycosylation (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4), and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with the mitochondrial membrane show a general pattern of decrease with age (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12).
source: We observed a general pattern of decrease with age for protein associated with oxidative phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8) and the mitochondrial membrane (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12), as well as protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5), glycosylation (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4), and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum show a general pattern of decrease with age (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5).
source: We observed a general pattern of decrease with age for protein associated with oxidative phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8) and the mitochondrial membrane (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12), as well as protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5), glycosylation (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4), and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with glycosylation show a general pattern of decrease with age (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4).
source: We observed a general pattern of decrease with age for protein associated with oxidative phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8) and the mitochondrial membrane (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12), as well as protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5), glycosylation (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4), and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with the endoplasmic reticulum membrane show a general pattern of decrease with age (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
source: We observed a general pattern of decrease with age for protein associated with oxidative phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−8) and the mitochondrial membrane (adjusted p-value = 2.2 × 10−12), as well as protein exit from the endoplasmic reticulum (adjusted p-value = 3.8 × 10−5), glycosylation (adjusted p-value = 2.6 × 10−4), and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane (adjusted p-value = 1.1 × 10−19).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes associated with the actin cytoskeleton show an overall increase with age (adjusted p-value = 4.2 × 10−5).
source: We observed an overall increase in genes associated with the actin cytoskeleton (adjusted p-value = 4.2 × 10−5).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with transmembrane transport show numerous changes, both increasing and decreasing with age (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−19).
source: We observed numerous changes, both increasing and decreasing with age, in proteins associated with transmembrane transport (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−19) and the plasma membrane (adjusted p-value = 3.4 × 10−6).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins associated with the plasma membrane show numerous changes, both increasing and decreasing with age (adjusted p-value = 3.4 × 10−6).
source: We observed numerous changes, both increasing and decreasing with age, in proteins associated with transmembrane transport (adjusted p-value = 1.7 × 10−19) and the plasma membrane (adjusted p-value = 3.4 × 10−6).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: There is an upregulation of transporters on the apical side of proximal tubule cells with age.
source: We see a significant upregulation with age of the transporters on the apical side (e.g. SLC5A2 [or SGLT2], SLC7A9, SLC10A2, SLC5A8, and SLC6A19), while at the same time a significant downregulation of transporters on the basolateral side (e.g. SLC2A1 [a.k.a. GLUT1], SLC26A1, SLC4A4, SLC12A6, SLC12A7, SLC13A3, and SLC19A1).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of cell-type specific proteins.

claim: There is a downregulation of transporters on the basolateral side of proximal tubule cells with age.
source: We see a significant upregulation with age of the transporters on the apical side (e.g. SLC5A2 [or SGLT2], SLC7A9, SLC10A2, SLC5A8, and SLC6A19), while at the same time a significant downregulation of transporters on the basolateral side (e.g. SLC2A1 [a.k.a. GLUT1], SLC26A1, SLC4A4, SLC12A6, SLC12A7, SLC13A3, and SLC19A1).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of cell-type specific proteins.

claim: Both subunits of the Na+/K+ ATP pump (ATP1A1 and ATP1B1) are significantly decreased with age.
source: Many of these basolateral transporters depend on ion gradients generated by the Na+/K+ ATP pump for their ability to function and both subunits of this pump (ATP1A1 and ATP1B1) are significantly decreased with age.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: VDAC1 is one of the key proteins that regulate mitochondrial function and is considered the gatekeeper for the passages of metabolites, nucleotides, and ions.
source: A picture of reduced proximal tubular function is completed by the overall decrease in many mitochondrial proteins, including VDAC1, which is one of the key proteins that regulate mitochondrial function and is considered the gatekeeper for the passages of metabolites, nucleotides, and ions (Camara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Camara et al., 2017.

claim: There is a decrease of proteins from all mitochondrial complexes as well as mitochondria-specific transporters with age.
source: We observe a decrease of proteins from all mitochondrial complexes as well as mitochondria-specific transporters.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: Remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton has a primary role in the structural adaptations made by podocytes to preserve their glomerular filtration properties.
source: Remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton has a primary role in the structural adaptations made by these cells to preserve their glomerular filtration properties.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about podocyte biology.

claim: Focal adhesions and slit diaphragms are signaling networks that interact with the actin cytoskeleton, maintain balance between intracellular and extracellular signals, and regulate podocyte function and morphology.
source: Focal adhesions and slit diaphragms are signaling networks that interact with the actin cytoskeleton, maintain balance between intracellular and extracellular signals, and regulate podocyte function and morphology (Perico et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Perico et al., 2016.

claim: Dystroglycan (DAG1) is decreased with age.
source: For the focal adhesions, we see a decrease in dystroglycan (DAG1), a protein that is highly abundant at the interface between the podocyte foot process and the glomerular basement membrane (GBM).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: Nephrin (NPHS1) and CD2AP are increased with age.
source: The slit diaphragm contains proteins that include nephrin (NPHS1) and CD2AP, both increased with age, and they regulate Cofilin (CFL1) activity, which is also increased and leads to stabilization of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: Cofilin (CFL1) is increased with age and leads to stabilization of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The slit diaphragm contains proteins that include nephrin (NPHS1) and CD2AP, both increased with age, and they regulate Cofilin (CFL1) activity, which is also increased and leads to stabilization of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: Actinin 4 (ACTN4) is increased with age.
source: We see an increase in actinin 4 (ACTN4), which crosslinks actin filaments in the podocyte and interacts with various other proteins.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: MYO1C and MYO1E are upregulated with age.
source: Two other upregulated proteins linking to the actin filaments and involved in filament organization are MYO1C and MYO1E.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: MYH9 is decreased with age.
source: Interesting, MYH9, which also interacts with actin filaments to contract the cytoskeleton, is decreased with age.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: AKT2 has an essential role in maintaining podocyte viability and normal cytoarchitecture after nephron loss.
source: AKT2, encoding the RACβ serine/threonine-protein kinase, has an essential role in maintaining podocyte viability and normal cytoarchitecture after nephron loss (Perico et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Perico et al., 2016.

claim: AKT2 is upregulated with age.
source: We see that AKT2 is upregulated with age.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of protein changes with age.

claim: Age-related changes in podocyte proteins suggest actin remodeling of the podocyte foot processes, which may be due to changes in glomerular filtration rate.
source: Overall, these changes with age suggest actin remodeling of the podocyte foot processes, which may be due to changes in glomerular filtration rate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the protein changes observed in podocytes.

claim: 1493 mRNAs show significant age trends (FDR < 0.1).
source: We identified significant (FDR < 0.1) age trends in 1493 mRNAs and 3871 proteins.
evidence: This is reported from statistical analysis comparing mRNA and protein changes.

claim: 3871 proteins show significant age trends (FDR < 0.1).
source: We identified significant (FDR < 0.1) age trends in 1493 mRNAs and 3871 proteins.
evidence: This is reported from statistical analysis comparing mRNA and protein changes.

claim: 5325 mRNAs show significant sex-specific differences (FDR < 0.1).
source: However, applying the same statistical criteria, we identified 5325 mRNAs and 4412 proteins with significant sex-specific differences.
evidence: This is reported from statistical analysis comparing mRNA and protein differences between sexes.

claim: 4412 proteins show significant sex-specific differences (FDR < 0.1).
source: However, applying the same statistical criteria, we identified 5325 mRNAs and 4412 proteins with significant sex-specific differences.
evidence: This is reported from statistical analysis comparing mRNA and protein differences between sexes.

claim: Age-related changes are more prevalent for proteins as compared to mRNA.
source: We conclude that age-related changes are more prevalent for proteins as compared to mRNA, consistent with our analysis of the PCs of variation described above.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing the numbers of significant changes in mRNA versus protein.

claim: The correlation of age-trends between mRNA and protein is r = 0.235 (p-value < 2.2 × 10−16).
source: The correlation of age-trends between mRNA and protein (r = 0.235, p-value < 2.2 × 10−16) is positive and highly significant but much smaller than the correlation of sex-specific differences (r = 0.626, p-value < 2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis of mRNA and protein changes.

claim: The correlation of sex-specific differences between mRNA and protein is r = 0.626 (p-value < 2.2 × 10−16).
source: The correlation of age-trends between mRNA and protein (r = 0.235, p-value < 2.2 × 10−16) is positive and highly significant but much smaller than the correlation of sex-specific differences (r = 0.626, p-value < 2.2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis of mRNA and protein changes.

claim: 309 genes show concordant increasing age-trends in both mRNA and protein (Group A).
source: We identified genes for mRNA and protein with age-trends that are concordant increasing (Group A, n = 309), discordant with mRNA decreasing and protein increasing (Group B, n = 196), discordant with mRNA increasing and protein decreasing (Group C, n = 108), and concordant decreasing (Group D, n = 359) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: 196 genes show discordant age-trends with mRNA decreasing and protein increasing (Group B).
source: We identified genes for mRNA and protein with age-trends that are concordant increasing (Group A, n = 309), discordant with mRNA decreasing and protein increasing (Group B, n = 196), discordant with mRNA increasing and protein decreasing (Group C, n = 108), and concordant decreasing (Group D, n = 359) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: 108 genes show discordant age-trends with mRNA increasing and protein decreasing (Group C).
source: We identified genes for mRNA and protein with age-trends that are concordant increasing (Group A, n = 309), discordant with mRNA decreasing and protein increasing (Group B, n = 196), discordant with mRNA increasing and protein decreasing (Group C, n = 108), and concordant decreasing (Group D, n = 359) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: 359 genes show concordant decreasing age-trends in both mRNA and protein (Group D).
source: We identified genes for mRNA and protein with age-trends that are concordant increasing (Group A, n = 309), discordant with mRNA decreasing and protein increasing (Group B, n = 196), discordant with mRNA increasing and protein decreasing (Group C, n = 108), and concordant decreasing (Group D, n = 359) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: 10.3% of genes have concordant age-related changes between mRNA and protein.
source: There are more genes with concordant changes (10.3%) but a substantial proportion of genes having changes with age occur in opposite directions (4.7%).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: 4.7% of genes have discordant age-related changes between mRNA and protein.
source: There are more genes with concordant changes (10.3%) but a substantial proportion of genes having changes with age occur in opposite directions (4.7%).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: Sex-specific differences are much more likely to be concordant (42.7%) between mRNA and protein.
source: Sex-specific differences are much more likely to be concordant (42.7%) with a relatively smaller proportion of discordant genes (11.7%) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of mRNA and protein sex differences.

claim: 11.7% of genes have discordant sex-specific differences between mRNA and protein.
source: Sex-specific differences are much more likely to be concordant (42.7%) with a relatively smaller proportion of discordant genes (11.7%) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of mRNA and protein sex differences.

claim: Among genes with concordant age-related increase in both mRNA and protein (Group A), the top enrichment categories are dominated by genes involved in the immune response, actin cytoskeleton organization, and cell adhesion.
source: Among the 309 genes with age-related increase in both mRNA and protein (Group A), the top enrichment categories are dominated by genes involved in the immune response, actin cytoskeleton organization, and cell adhesion.
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis of Group A genes.

claim: Group A includes concordant increases in the immuno-proteosome complex (e.g., Psmb8, Psmb9, Psmb10, and Psme1).
source: We also observed concordant increases in the immuno-proteosome complex (e.g., Psmb8, Psmb9, Psmb10, and Psme1).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Group A genes.

claim: Among genes with concordant age-related decrease in mRNA and protein (Group D), there is enrichment of genes involved in transmembrane transport, mitochondrial membrane, and Golgi vesicle transport.
source: Among the 359 genes that had a concordant age-related decrease in mRNA and protein (Group D) we see enrichment of genes involved in transmembrane transport, mitochondrial membrane, Golgi vesicle transport that were noted previously.
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis of Group D genes.

claim: Group D includes enrichment of genes involved in junction formation including cadherins, catenins, and claudins.
source: We also see enrichment of genes involved in junction formation including cadherins (Cdh16), catenins (Ctnnb1 and Ctnnd1), and claudins (Cldn8, Cldn10).
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis of Group D genes.

claim: Cell-cell junctions become leaky with age in other tissues.
source: Although there is no direct evidence in the kidney, it has been shown that these junctions become leaky with age in other tissues (Jeong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Jeong et al., 2017.

claim: Several proteins in ubiquitin mediated protein catabolism are concordantly downregulated with age.
source: Several proteins in ubiquitin mediated protein catabolism are concordantly downregulated (Ubac2, Ube3c, Ubqln4, Ubr4, Usp20, Usp32, Usp33, Usp34, Usp39, and Usp9x).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Group D genes.

claim: Klotho is concordantly downregulated with age.
source: Notable among the genes in this category is Klotho, an aging-suppressor gene primarily expressed in the kidney.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Group D genes.

claim: Klotho is an aging-suppressor gene primarily expressed in the kidney.
source: Notable among the genes in this category is Klotho, an aging-suppressor gene primarily expressed in the kidney.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Klotho.

claim: Klotho is associated with fibrosis and is an antagonist of beta catenin.
source: Klotho is associated with fibrosis and is an antagonist of beta catenin (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: Klotho knockout mice exhibit increased incidence of aging-related diseases including atherosclerosis, vascular and tissue calcification, and CKD.
source: Previous studies have shown that Klotho knockout mice exhibit increased incidence of aging-related diseases including atherosclerosis, vascular and tissue calcification, and CKD (Bolignano et al., 2014; Kuro-o et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Bolignano et al., 2014 and Kuro-o et al., 1997.

claim: Decreased Klotho expression has been shown to drive accelerated aging.
source: Decreased Klotho expression has been shown to drive accelerated aging (Kurosu, 2005) and renal failure (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Kurosu, 2005.

claim: Decreased Klotho expression has been shown to drive renal failure.
source: Decreased Klotho expression has been shown to drive accelerated aging (Kurosu, 2005) and renal failure (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: 196 genes show decreasing mRNA and increasing protein levels with age (Group B).
source: We identified 196 genes with decreasing mRNA and increasing protein levels with age (Group B).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: Group B includes genes exclusively localized to the brush border of the proximal tubule that are important for reabsorption of specific metabolites.
source: This group includes genes that are exclusively localized to the brush border of the proximal tubule (e.g., Slc26a6, Slc34a3, Slc5a2, Slc3a1, Slc9a3, Pdzk1, and Lrp2) and are important for the reabsorption of specific metabolites in the ultrafiltrate.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Group B genes.

claim: SGLT2 (encoded by Slc5a2) is responsible for 97% of glucose reabsorption.
source: The glucose transporter SGLT2 (encoded by Slc5a2) is responsible for 97% of glucose reabsorption (Vallon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Vallon et al., 2011.

claim: SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 together form the antiporter that mediates uptake of cysteine.
source: SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 together form the antiporter that mediates uptake of cysteine, which is of particular interest because of the potential role of cysteine in aging (Flurkey et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Flurkey et al., 2010.

claim: Lrp2 encodes Megalin, the receptor that exclusively mediates albumin reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
source: Lrp2 encodes Megalin, the receptor that exclusively mediates albumin reabsorption in the proximal tubule and can affect the amount of albumin in the urine (see below).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Megalin function.

claim: PDZK1 is a scaffold protein that connects membrane proteins and regulatory components at the apical side.
source: PDZK1 is a scaffold protein that connects membrane proteins and regulatory components at the apical side and has been shown to interact with several transporters in Group B, such as Slc9a3 encoding the main sodium-hydrogen antiporter (NHE3), responsible for sodium balance (Zachos et al., 2009), Slc22a6, encoding OAT1, which plays a central role in organic anion transport, and Slc34a1 and Slc34a3, encoding transporters important for phosphate transport (see below) (Lanaspa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zachos et al., 2009 and Lanaspa et al., 2007.

claim: 109 genes show increasing mRNA and decreasing protein with age (Group C).
source: We identified 109 genes with increasing mRNA and decreasing protein (Group C).
evidence: This is reported from comparison of mRNA and protein age trends.

claim: Group C is highly enriched for cytosolic ribosome including >20 genes from both small and large subunits.
source: This group is highly enriched for cytosolic ribosome including >20 genes from both small and large subunits.
evidence: This is reported from functional enrichment analysis of Group C genes.

claim: Group C includes genes involved in RNA splicing (Srsf3, Srsf5, Srsf6, and Snrpa1).
source: Group C also includes genes Srsf3, Srsf5, Srsf6, and Snrpa1 that are involved in RNA splicing.
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Group C genes.

claim: Downregulation of splicing factor SRSF3 has been shown to induce alternative splicing of TP53 that results in cellular senescence.
source: Downregulation of splicing factor, SRSF3, has been shown to induce alternative splicing of TP53 that results in cellular senescence (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tang et al., 2013.

claim: Within each age category the correlations of mRNAs with their corresponding proteins are predominantly positive.
source: Within each age category the correlations of mRNAs with their corresponding proteins are predominantly positive.
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis within age groups.

claim: While RNA and protein are usually correlated within age groups, the relative balance between RNA and protein can change in any direction across age groups.
source: Thus, while RNA and protein are usually correlated within age groups, the relative balance between RNA and protein can change in any direction across age groups.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of mRNA-protein relationships across ages.

claim: Age-related changes in protein levels are not necessarily due to transcriptional regulation and may not track age-related changes in RNA.
source: This suggests that age-related changes in protein levels are not necessarily due to transcriptional regulation and may not track age-related changes in RNA.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of mRNA-protein relationships across ages.

claim: Mediation analysis shows essentially no change in the significance of the age effect on protein after accounting for mRNA.
source: However, we observe essentially no change in the significance of the age effect on protein and conclude that the age-related changes in protein occur independently of changes in mRNA.
evidence: This is reported from mediation analysis comparing protein ~ age models with and without mRNA.

claim: Age-related changes in protein occur independently of changes in mRNA.
source: However, we observe essentially no change in the significance of the age effect on protein and conclude that the age-related changes in protein occur independently of changes in mRNA.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from mediation analysis.

claim: Sex-specific differences in protein are reduced after accounting for mRNA, consistent with a model in which sex-specific differences in protein are a direct response to sex-specific differences in mRNA.
source: Here we see that significance of the sex effect on proteins is reduced after accounting for mRNA, for most genes. This is consistent with a model in which sex-specific differences in protein are a direct response to sex-specific differences in mRNA.
evidence: This is reported from mediation analysis of sex effects on protein.

claim: The processes that drive age-related change in proteins are post-translational and may involve specific changes in translational efficiency or rates of mRNA or protein turnover.
source: This suggests that the processes that drive age-related change in proteins are post-translational and may involve specific changes in translational efficiency (Anisimova et al., 2020) or rates of mRNA or protein turnover (Cellerino and Ori, 2017).
evidence: This is concluded from the mediation analysis with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Pdzk1ip1 is the protein most strongly correlated with urinary phosphate (r = 0.322, p-value = 7.5 × 10−5 adjusted for sex).
source: The protein most strongly correlated with urinary phosphate is Pdzk1ip1 (r = 0.322, p-value = 7.5 × 10−5 adjusted for sex; r = 0.32, p-value = 0.0027 adjusted for sex and age) (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis of proteins with urinary phenotypes.

claim: Pdzk1ip1 is expressed specifically in proximal tubule cells in segment S2.
source: Pdzk1ip1 is expressed specifically in proximal tubule cells in segment S2 (Lake et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lake et al., 2019.

claim: After accounting for Pdzk1ip1 protein levels, age is no longer a significant predictor of urinary phosphate (p-value = 0.22).
source: We fit a multivariable regression model to urinary phosphate and noted that after accounting for Pdzk1ip1 protein levels, age is no longer a significant predictor of urinary phosphate (p-value for age is 0.22 adjusted for PDZK1IP1).
evidence: This is reported from multivariable regression analysis.

claim: Pdzk1ip1 is a mediator (or a close surrogate) for the change in urinary phosphate levels with age.
source: This is consistent with a causal for Pdzk1ip1 as a mediator (or a close surrogate) for the change in urinary phosphate levels with age.
evidence: This is concluded from the multivariable regression analysis.

claim: 799 proteins are significantly correlated with Pdzk1ip1 (adjusted p-value < 0.05) and are enriched for membrane transporters and proteins associated with the brush border and apical side of the cell.
source: We examined the set of 799 proteins that are significantly correlated with Pdzk1ip1 (adjusted p-value < 0.05) and found these to be enriched for membrane transporters and other proteins associated with the brush border and apical side of the cell.
evidence: This is reported from correlation and enrichment analysis.

claim: Protein levels of NPT2A (Slc34a1) and NPT2C (Slc34a3) do not correlate with urinary phosphate excretion.
source: Interestingly, protein levels of NPT2A (Slc34a1) and NPT2C (Slc34a3) that form the major sodium-phosphate co-transporter do not correlate with urinary phosphate excretion (Figure 8B and C), confirming that phosphate reabsorption by this transporter is not regulated by the protein level of the subunits and instead by their interactions with PDZK1 and PDZK1IP1 (Giral et al., 2011).
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis with citation to Giral et al., 2011.

claim: Megalin (encoded by Lrp2) is the receptor that mediates albumin reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
source: Megalin, the protein encoded by Lrp2, is the receptor that mediates albumin reabsorption in the proximal tubule.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Megalin function.

claim: Lrp2 shows a decrease in mRNA expression (p-value = 2.4 × 10−5) and an increase in protein level (p-value = 0.0043) with age.
source: It is another Group B gene that shows a decrease in both mRNA expression (p-value = 2.4 × 10−5), an increase in protein level (p-value = 0.0043) with age and a positive correlation between mRNA and protein levels within each age group (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of Lrp2 mRNA and protein changes.

claim: 157 of the 188 animals had albumin levels below 1 mg/dL.
source: The majority of animals in our DO cohort do not show albuminuria – 157 of the 188 animals had albumin levels below 1 mg/dL – and although this limits our ability to draw conclusions regarding the relationship between urinary albumin levels and Megalin expression levels, Megalin is negatively correlated with albumin (p-value = 0.081 after regression adjustment for sex and age) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is reported from analysis of urinary albumin measurements.

claim: Megalin is negatively correlated with albumin (p-value = 0.081 after regression adjustment for sex and age).
source: The majority of animals in our DO cohort do not show albuminuria – 157 of the 188 animals had albumin levels below 1 mg/dL – and although this limits our ability to draw conclusions regarding the relationship between urinary albumin levels and Megalin expression levels, Megalin is negatively correlated with albumin (p-value = 0.081 after regression adjustment for sex and age) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is reported from correlation analysis.

claim: The direction of change of a protein with age cannot be reliably predicted based on changes in its coding mRNA even for genes where the mRNA and protein are correlated within age groups.
source: While others have reported that mRNA can be a poor proxy for protein abundance (Liu et al., 2016), we find that the direction of change of a protein with age cannot be reliably predicted based on changes in its coding mRNA even for genes where the mRNA and protein are correlated within age groups.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of mRNA-protein relationships with citation to Liu et al., 2016.

claim: A recent study in which RNAseq and Riboseq data was compared in kidneys in 3-, 20-, and 32-month-old male C57BL/6 mice concluded no significant changes in translation rates between time points.
source: However, a recent study in which RNAseq and Riboseq data was compared in kidneys in 3-, 20-, and 32-month-old male C57BL/6 mice concluded no significant changes in translation rates between time points (Anisimova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Anisimova et al., 2020.

claim: Loss of proteostasis is a hallmark of aging that manifests at the cellular level in a number of ways, such as protein aggregation, unfolding, oxidative damage, post-translational modification, and altered rates of protein turnover.
source: Loss of proteostasis is a hallmark of aging that manifests at the cellular level in a number of ways, such as protein aggregation, unfolding, oxidative damage, post-translational modification, and altered rates of protein turnover (Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Labbadia and Morimoto, 2014.

claim: There is a decrease in correlation between protein subunits of the 26S proteasome complex in the heart of DO mice with age.
source: We recently found a decrease in correlation between protein subunits of the 26S proteasome complex in the heart of DO mice with age, suggesting that loss of stoichiometry of the proteasome system itself may contribute to the decline in the protein quality control process during aging (Gyuricza, 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Gyuricza, 2020.

claim: Age-related changes in protein and mRNA appear to be uncoupled, despite that protein and mRNA remain coupled within age groups.
source: Age-related changes in protein and mRNA appear to be uncoupled, despite that protein and mRNA remain coupled within age groups.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of mRNA-protein relationships.

claim: Changes in protein homeostasis in aging animals occur as a result of changes in post-transcriptional processes – through changes in translation efficiency or of protein turnover.
source: Our findings suggest that changes in protein homeostasis in aging animals occur as a result of changes in post-transcriptional processes – through changes in translation efficiency or of protein turnover.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of mRNA-protein relationships.

claim: The initial cohort consisted of 600 DO mice (300 males and 300 females) bred at The Jackson Laboratory.
source: Our initial cohort consisted of 600 DO mice (300 males and 300 females) bred at The Jackson Laboratory (stock no. 009376) in five breeding waves (generations 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the study cohort.

claim: DO mice are a genetically diverse, outbred population derived from eight founder strains that together contribute >50 million well-characterized variants.
source: The DO mice are a genetically diverse, outbred population derived from eight founder strains that together contribute >50 million well-characterized variants (Svenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Svenson et al., 2012.
